sections.overview: The Great Knot is the largest Calidris sandpiper, breeding in subarctic eastern Siberia and migrating to coastal East Asia and Australasia, especially north-western Australia.
sections.identification: At roughly 26–28 cm, it is a stocky, long-billed shorebird; breeding adults show dense black spotting on the breast and flanks, while non-breeding plumage is greyer and plainer.
sections.habitat: It breeds on high subarctic plateaus with lichen, herbs and dwarf shrubs, then uses sheltered bays, estuaries and expansive intertidal mudflats during migration and winter.
sections.diet: Its food changes with season: berries and pine seeds are reported on the breeding grounds, whereas migrating and wintering birds take bivalves, gastropods, crustaceans and worms from tidal flats.
sections.behavior: It is a long-distance migrant that gathers in large, sometimes mixed flocks at a small number of coastal staging areas.
sections.reproduction: The female lays a clutch of three or four eggs in a tundra scrape, and the male provides most of the care after hatching, according to Australian government species material.
sections.ecology: Like the much smaller Red-necked Stint (C. ruficollis), it depends on the East Asian–Australasian Flyway, but its larger body, different seasonal diet and dependence on abundant molluscs at key stopovers distinguish its ecology.
sections.conservation: The IUCN Red List assessment published in 2025 lists the species as Endangered, with a decreasing population and continuing loss or degradation of coastal staging habitat.
